newsitem.title: USA: U.S. union membership decline continues in 1996.
newsitem.headline: U.S. union membership decline continues in 1996.

text.p: The number of American workers who belonged to unions shrank last year, continuing a downward trend that began in the late 1970s, the Labour Department reported on Friday.

Union membership fell in 1996 to 16.3 million, or 14.5 percent of wage and salary employees, from 16.4 million workers, or 14.9 percent, in 1995, the Labour Department said. Another 1.9 million workers were covered by union contracts, but were not union members, it said.
The decline came despite an ongoing massive effort by the new leadership of the AFL-CIO and many of its 78 affiliated unions to organise workers.
Organised labour's share of the workforce began a downward drift after peaking in the 1950s when about one-third of all workers carried union cards.
The decline accelerated in the late 1970s and through the 1980s as jobs in the heavily unionized manufacturing sector vanished mostly because of global competition and automation.
After declining for 14 years in a row, the number of union members rose slightly in 1993 and 1994 to 16.75 million, but has resumed its downward trend since then.

Even in years when union membership has increased, it has failed to keep pace with the growth of wage and salary workers, which rose 1.7 percent last year to 112 million. The total, however, includes supervisers, managers and top executives who are not eligible for union membership under U.S. labour law.

Union membership in the non-farm private sector was little changed at 9.4 million workers last year, but as a percentage of the 92.1 million private sector workers, it fell to 10.2 percent from 10.4 percent in 1995, the department said.
Among the 18.2 million government workers, union membership was little changed last year at 6.9 million, or 37.7 percent.

Private industries with the highest proportion of union members were transportation and public utilities, followed by construction, manufacturing and mining, the department said. Occupations with the lowest union percentages were technical, administrative support and agricultural, it said.
Black men were the most heavily unionized with 21.6 perent, while white women were the least at 11.3 percent, it said.
Union members' median weekly earnings of $615 were about one-third higher than the $462 for workers not represented by unions, the department said.
